title: Feeling Good
author: David D. Burns
theme: Our moods are shaped largely by the way we think about events, so learning to notice and correct distorted thoughts can lift low feelings and build lasting self-respect.
takeaway: This week, when you feel upset, write down the exact thought running through your mind, name the thinking error in it, and write a fairer, more balanced thought beside it.
summary: David Burns, a psychiatrist, wrote this book to bring the methods of cognitive therapy, developed by his mentor Aaron Beck, to ordinary readers. His message is hopeful: low moods, worry and self-criticism are not simply things that happen to us. Much of how we feel comes from what we tell ourselves about what happens.

The core idea is that thoughts come before feelings. When someone feels worthless or hopeless, the thoughts behind that feeling are often unfair and one-sided, even though they seem completely true in the moment. Burns describes a set of common thinking errors, such as seeing things as all-or-nothing, turning one setback into a never-ending pattern, filtering out the good, jumping to conclusions, harsh labels, and loading ourselves with endless shoulds.

His main tool is simple and practical. On paper, you write down the upsetting thought, identify the distortion in it, and then write a more realistic response. Doing this regularly, rather than just thinking about it, is what makes the difference. Small steps and daily activity records also help break the cycle of doing nothing and feeling worse.

Burns also tackles deeper habits. He argues that self-worth does not have to be earned through success, approval or love from others, and that perfectionism quietly makes people unhappy. He offers ways to handle criticism calmly, to cool down anger, and to separate healthy regret from crushing guilt.

For family life, the lessons are very useful. Parents and partners often react not to what someone did but to the meaning they read into it. Catching thoughts like he never listens or I am a terrible mother gives everyone room to respond more kindly. The book does not replace professional care for serious depression, but it shows that clearer thinking can bring real relief.

questions.q: What is the central idea of Feeling Good?
options: Moods are mainly caused by brain chemistry and cannot be changed by effort
Our feelings are largely shaped by the way we think about events
Happiness depends mostly on outside circumstances
Strong emotions should always be expressed immediately
questions.why: Burns teaches that thoughts come before feelings, so changing distorted thoughts can change moods.

questions.q: Which form of therapy does the book bring to general readers?
options: Psychoanalysis
Hypnotherapy
Family systems therapy
Cognitive therapy
questions.why: The book popularises cognitive therapy, developed by Aaron Beck, Burns's mentor.

questions.q: Seeing a situation as either total success or total failure is an example of which thinking error?
options: All-or-nothing thinking
Emotional reasoning
Personalization
Disqualifying the positive
questions.why: All-or-nothing thinking sees things in black and white, with no middle ground.

questions.q: What is the main practical tool Burns recommends for handling upsetting thoughts?
options: Ignoring the thoughts until they fade
Talking the thoughts over with as many friends as possible
Writing the thought down, naming its distortion, and writing a more realistic response
Replacing every negative thought with a cheerful slogan
questions.why: Burns stresses written practice: record the thought, spot the error, and answer it with a fairer one.

questions.q: According to Burns, where does true self-worth come from?
options: It does not have to be earned through achievement, approval or love
It comes from being praised by others
It depends on career success
It grows only from being in a loving relationship
questions.why: Burns argues that self-worth is not something we must earn through success or other people's approval.

questions.q: Taking one setback and treating it as a never-ending pattern of defeat is called:
options: Mental filter
Overgeneralization
Labeling
Magnification
questions.why: Overgeneralization turns a single negative event into a sweeping rule about life.

questions.q: What does Burns say about perfectionism?
options: It is the surest path to happiness
It is necessary for high achievement
It only affects people at work
It quietly makes people unhappy and anxious
questions.why: Burns sees perfectionism as a self-defeating habit that leads to stress and disappointment.

questions.q: Why does Burns suggest planning small activities and recording them when feeling low?
options: To keep busy so there is no time to think
To prove to others that one is not lazy
To break the cycle of inactivity that makes low moods worse
To earn rewards from a therapist
questions.why: Doing small tasks counters the inactivity that feeds depression and gives evidence against hopeless thoughts.

questions.q: Believing something must be true simply because you feel it strongly is called:
options: Emotional reasoning
Fortune telling
Should statements
Minimization
questions.why: Emotional reasoning treats feelings as proof of facts, such as feeling stupid and concluding one is stupid.

questions.q: How can the book's ideas help in family relationships?
options: By teaching family members to avoid all disagreements
By showing that only children's thinking needs correcting
By helping people notice the unfair meanings they read into a loved one's actions
By encouraging parents to hide their feelings completely
questions.why: Catching distorted thoughts about partners or children lets people respond more calmly and kindly.
